text: Councils turn to AI in attempt to fill £4bn black hole Prime minister Andy Burnham has pledged to reform social care in the UK as dozens of councils look to make drastic cuts to their care provision Councils across the UK are increasingly turning towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) as they try to fill a looming Â£4bn financial black hole. But local government experts say it is not the "silver bullet" to save a system from "the brink of collapse". There are also ethical concerns around the increasing use of AI in assessing the level of care vulnerable people need. A government spokesman said it encouraged safe and responsible use of the technology where it could reduce workloads. A study by the BBC Shared Data Unit found all but a small handful of the UK's local authorities will reduce the services they offer this financial year, despite recent reforms to the way they are funded. The 218 upper-tier councils, which include borough, county, metropolitan and unitary authorities, will make a total of Â£3.2bn in cuts. Planned measures include reducing the frequency of bin collections, closing heritage attractions, ending bus routes and - in the case of one council - completely removing sheltered housing support. Fees and charges for parking permits and green waste bins will be hiked at dozens of councils, while almost every authority will raise council tax by the maximum 5%. Jonathan Carr West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), which advises on policy across the world, said the BBC study showed the sector was "still struggling to keep up with astronomic rates of increase in demand and cost for those key statutory services like adult social care and children's services". "The sector as a whole continues to become more and more on the brink of collapse," he added. A spokesman for the Local Government Association, which represents councils across England and Wales, said the cost and demand pressures were "unrelenting". "In just three years, councils will need around 25 per cent more money simply to stand still," he said. "Without action, the services people rely on every day, from social care to safe streets, will be eroded." Though the government has increased the amount of grant funding councils receive from the Treasury since the pandemic, a study by independent thinktank the Institute for Government found it was still , external down on pre-2010 levels , external . Even if this year's savings are achieved, councils predict they will need to find a further Â£3.8bn by the end of the 2027-28 financial year to balance their books. A record 37 councils will also receive forms of exceptional financial support this year. It means many are trying to lower the cost of providing care to the elderly and vulnerable, whether by re-tendering contracts with cheaper care companies, closing care homes or by re-assessing those already in care to see if their package of support can be reduced. Adult social care - the largest expenditure of almost every upper-tier council in the UK - is set to bear the brunt of cuts this year This year, dozens of councils have pledged to use AI to drive savings. Among them are Medway Council chiefs who say they will use AI to "draft care plans" and automate invoice processing. Several councils will reduce staffing in their call centres - which enable people to query council tax bills, order new bins or arrange a care assessment among other things - and bring in chatbots to "triage" initial queries. West Sussex County Council hopes its plans to replace nine call handlers with an AI contact centre could save Â£300,000 a year. But campaigners for the elderly say older people are already struggling to interact with automated chatbots where they have been introduced. Similar measures have proved controversial in other areas. Derby's AI chatbot Darcie received several complaints for struggling to understand the local accent . Dennis Reed, director of the Silver Voices campaign group for elderly people, said: "People seeking social care support are likely to be confused, perhaps in pain, and not used to negotiating the merry-go-round of contact centres using AI at first contact. "What potential social care clients need at first contact is a sympathetic human voice, not a robotic answering machine." Denise Rowley, 71, previously taught IT among other subjects to older people at a college in Leeds. After suffering a stroke nearly a decade ago, she has relied on Wakefield Council's trips and falls service Carelink to help her if she gets into difficulty. But with the Department for Work and Pensions expanding its AI-assisted call centre and local councils following suit, she says older people are increasingly feeling shut out by new technology when contacting services they need. "Older people do struggle with technology," Rowley said. "It's bad enough having to use computers every time you need something, let alone having to talk to an AI. "And the thing is, a lot of these AI call centres are based on a system that didn't work in the first place." LGIU chief executive Jonathan Carr-West says councils remain in a perilous financial situation despite recent reforms Councils and care providers are already using AI to write case notes, predict falls and analyse care records. But there are serious concerns around the use of such tools to draft care assessments, where social workers record a person's needs and decide what council-funded support they are entitled to. "This is something our members are really worried about," said Andrew Reece, strategic lead for the British Association of Social Workers. "This is stepping into the area of making decisions and we don't think that's appropriate." He said it was different to tools that assisted social workers - for example, recording a conversation to help them make good notes. The use of AI to create assessments would be "stepping over the boundary between assisting a social worker and taking over from them", he said. Derby City Council said its AI-drafted care assessments were always reviewed by a social worker. But a report by the Ada Lovelace Institute , external found AI tools made frequent errors in care assessments, some of which found their way into finalised reports. Reece was also concerned to see AI being trumpeted as a means to save money. "The system is under a huge amount of pressure at the moment and most social workers are not able to complete their work within their normal hours," he added. "The savings will come from shedding social work jobs, which will just put more pressure on the system." In some cases, the expected savings are relatively small. Liverpool's use of AI tools to improve efficiency in children's social care will save about Â£150,000 by the end of the 2027-28 financial year. In proportion, its total budget gap during the same time is more than Â£29m. "There is no silver bullet," said Carr-West. "We have seen some savings being made from AI, but they are, to be frank, pretty marginal compared to the scale of the problem." Councils across England said they were increasingly looking to technology and AI to help manage mounting financial pressures, as demand for social care, homelessness support and special educational needs services continues to rise. Caerphilly Council said its transformation programme included the use of technology and AI to make services more efficient, while Essex County Council said it was exploring further savings through "technology and digitisation" and redesigning services. Council's AI helpers only resolve half of cases AI plan unveiled to cut council tenant rent debts AI could flag issues with council homes sooner A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the government did not mandate how local authorities used AI, but encouraged its use where it could help "alleviate pressures and free up staff to help deliver better public services". Many authorities said digital reform would help to balance future budgets, but warned technology alone would not solve wider funding pressures. Across the UK, council chiefs said budgets were being severely stretched by the spiraling cost of providing care, homelessness services and supporting looked after children as well as providing home to school transport. Barnet Council has one of the largest budget gaps in the UK for its size and will need close to Â£80m of government support this year. Describing the council as a "tightly run ship", a spokesperson said it had faced "the perfect storm" of a decade of reduced government funding and year-on-year rises in service costs. Six of the 10 councils set to make the most savings per head of population in 2026-27 are London boroughs, adding to fears town halls within the capital are being hit hardest , external by rising costs. Carr-West said there had been hope Labour's recent local government reforms would begin to improve the situation. It has introduced multi-year funding settlements, effectively telling councils how much they will get several years in advance rather than just the next year. It also made drastic changes to the formula used to allocate funds, with more money directed towards areas assessed as having higher levels of need and less ability to raise income locally through council tax. "If we're all marching towards a cliff edge, they've sort of slightly slowed down that progress, but they haven't fundamentally changed its direction," added Carr-West. In July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders. The government is set to press ahead with plans to replace two-tier council areas with single councils responsible for all local services, in what ministers say will simplify local government. The changes are also intended to save money by reducing duplication and cutting administrative costs. The MHCLG spokesman said: "We're making Â£78bn available to local authorities across the country this year through our fair funding settlement â and thanks to our changes, nine in 10 councils in England will receive funding that matches their relative need by the end of 2028-29." text: Reform's leader in Scotland Malcolm Offord reveals cancer diagnosis Malcolm Offord said he had a procedure last week to remove his prostate Reform UK's leader in Scotland has revealed he was diagnosed with prostate cancer on the day of the Holyrood election on 7 May. Malcolm Offord said he had a procedure last week to remove his prostate and was now "clear" and "raring to go". Speaking to comedian Matt Forde at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, he said being diagnosed with cancer was a "scary thing" and urged men to "just get checked". Offord, a former Conservative peer, led Reform to a Scottish Parliament breakthrough in May with 17 seats. He told Forde that being diagnosed with cancer was "scary". But he added: "I've got a couple of pals who have been through this, so it doesn't hold the same level of fear. "I think the benefit is people now talking about this, particularly men who didn't talk about this in the past." Offord said he was "feeling pretty good" after surgery. "The thing about the prostate is it is out and gone, I can move on," he said. "But the point is it is pretty routine, I am 61 years old, about to become 62, it happens in a lot of men that age. "The good news is that medics are all over this, they know what they are doing, they know how to fix this, they can fix it fast and there is plenty of life after that." Offord urged men to "just get checked". Reform's Scottish Parliament success in May left Offord as leader of the joint-second biggest party at Holyrood. title: Reform's leader in Scotland Malcolm Offord reveals cancer diagnosis

text: Male prisons in England and Wales have fewer than 1,800 spaces Male prisons have fewer than 1,800 spaces available in England and Wales, the lowest level since March. More than 83,000 spaces are occupied by male inmates, despite the government introducing a presumption against jailing anyone for under one year to free up more space. Prison staff told the BBC the high level of offenders being recalled to prison for breaching licence conditions given on their release or re-offending has cancelled out much of the extra room. Since June, there has been a downward trend in the number of vacant spaces. The spike comes before the government is set to release about 5,000 inmates early from October to alleviate overcrowding. Plan to scrap most short jail terms comes into effect PM asks justice secretary to find way to keep PC Harper's killers in jail The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it was building more prisons while exploring early release options and expanding electronic tagging. The figures come after Prime Minister Andy Burnham made more prisoners exempt from the upcoming early release scheme following backlash from victims. Burnham came under further pressure after the killers of PC Andrew Harper would still be eligible for early release. PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire. Last week, Burnham said he was "confident" PC Harper's killers could be excluded from the government's early release scheme On August 3, Burnham said in a written article , external he had "wanted to go even further" but had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do". A spokesperson for the MoJ said "public safety will always be our priority". "We are fast-tracking a plan to keep more of the most serious offenders behind bars, on top of murderers, anyone on life sentences and those in prison for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences who are already blocked from any changes," they said. "We share the public's anger that these options are even being considered, after we inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse."
title: Male prisons in England and Wales have fewer than 1,800 spaces

text: Reform suspends councillor ahead of court case Reform UK said Glenn Gibbins had been suspended from the party Reform UK has suspended a councillor pending the outcome of an offensive message court case. Last month, Sunderland City councillor Glenn Gibbins, 66, was charged with posting a grossly offensive comment on social media in connection to a comment referencing the Nigerian community. The charge, under the Communications Act 2003, related to a post from 2024. Gibbins is due to appear at South Tyneside Magistrates' Court on Friday. A Reform spokesperson said: "Councillor Gibbins has been suspended from Reform UK pending the outcome of his case." Northumbria Police began an investigation when the post came to light in May. Gibbins was elected to the council that same month and was then suspended by Reform, before being reinstated with a final written warning. After he was charged, the party suspended him again and he is listed on the Sunderland City Council website as an Independent. Reform did not confirm when it had suspended the councillor, or the reason why. Follow BBC Sunderland on X , external , Facebook , external , Nextdoor and Instagram , external . text: Trial of facts over ex-mayor's 'bigoted' tweets Pat Marsh is the subject of a trial of facts over alleged antisemitic tweets A former North Yorkshire councillor who also served as the mayor of Harrogate posted antisemitic tweets which were "greater than bigotry in the extreme", a court heard. Pat Marsh, 78, is accused of stirring up racial hatred by publishing written material in relation to posts made on X in January and February 2024. A trial of facts is taking place at York Crown Court as Marsh, who has dementia, has been deemed physically and mentally unfit to enter a plea and give evidence as part of a conventional trial. The trial of facts, which has yet to hear evidence in her defence, is expected to conclude on Friday. Opening the case earlier, prosecutor Ashleigh Metcalfe said most of the content which Marsh posted on X while a serving councillor was "concerned with the events in Gaza and was plainly anti-Israel", adding: "Some of it was antisemitic". "We say it's greater than bigotry in the extreme," she said. The posts attracted hundreds of views, said Metcalfe, who told jurors they were later picked up by local and national media outlets, thereby expanding their reach. She said the tweets were "threatening, abusive or insulting [and] in all circumstances likely to stir up racial hatred". Marsh, who has no previous convictions, was arrested on 20 February 2024 after police received four reports about the alleged antisemitic posts. She did not answer any questions put to her in a police interview later that day, the court heard. Following her arrest, Marsh, who represented the Stray, Woodlands and Hookstone ward as a councillor in Harrogate, resigned from her post after three decades in public life. She was also suspended by her party, the Liberal Democrats. According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , she had denied the posts were antisemitic prior to being charged. text: Wildfire 'overlooked' as it was in the North - MP Alison Hume, pictured in early 2026 near the North York Moors wildfire site, says a national conversation has now begun A "huge and devastating" wildfire in the North York Moors last year was "overlooked" by the government and national media because it was in the north of England, a Labour MP has said. Alison Hume's Scarborough and Whitby constituency includes the 10 sq mile (25 sq km) area of Langdale Moor which was ravaged by a fire which burned for more than 40 days. "There was very little interest from the national media," she said, adding that in recent weeks there had been "smaller wildfires in the South that received a lot of coverage". The government said it was "supporting every part of the country that has been affected by wildfire - not just the South". Hume said she had been "surprised" that national news outlets did not cover the Fylingdales fire "for weeks". "It's been very noticeable that since there's been wildfires in the South, the coverage has gone through the roof." Hume added that she "wouldn't want to draw anything away from how serious" a blaze in Stourbridge was last week. "With the 19 homes totally destroyed, that was off the scale and devastating," she said. On Friday, the prime minister said emergency services were responding to 37 wildfires, with major incidents spread across the southern half of the UK. Hume said she was "really pleased" that Andy Burnham had announced a temporary ban on disposable barbecues and that an emergency alert was sent to people's phones warning of a "very high risk of wildfires". "Of course I'm glad that we're getting more national interest in wildfires," she said. "The country's now coming to terms with something that we've been coming to terms with in North Yorkshire for a while, which is when you get a wildfire, it doesn't end when the fire's put out." Efforts to "rebuild the community" were continuing one year on from the North York Moors fire, she said. Hume welcomed government funding to help cover North Yorkshire Fire & Rescue Service's expenses from the wildfire, and Â£3.2m towards moorland recovery. But she said the financial loss suffered by farmers and other businesses had "slipped through the cracks". "I think had it been in the South, my calls for an extension of the grant network, which exists for flooding, would have probably been better received," she said. "We can't ask our community to turn out, put their lives on the line in many cases, stand shoulder to shoulder with our fire and rescue services, help put the fires out and then say, 'well, I'm sorry your tractor was damaged' or 'I'm sorry your business was closed'." Hume, who founded and leads the All Party Parliamentary Group on Wildfires, said she had since had "conversations with government about really getting them to look at how they support people affected by wildfires afterwards". "We're learning a lot from last year and I'm hoping that that learning can also be extended throughout the country," she said. "I don't want to go on about the North-South divide, but we know there is one, right?" 10 sq miles (25 sq km) of North Yorkshire moorland was damaged, pictured here in February 2026 Hume also called for ministers to "really look at what happens when fire gets close to a piece of critical national infrastructure". Last summer's wildfire burned near to RAF Fylingdales, part of the UK and US ballistic missile warning system. She said she had visited the site this week and spoke to staff who "can't just turn the radar off and leave". "It was quite sobering to hear how worried they were as the fire got closer." Last month, a wildfire in Suffolk was about 3 miles (5km) from the Sizewell B nuclear power station. Hume said such situations should automatically trigger national resilience, when firefighters from brigades around the country are sent to assist. "Extra resources come in at that point where something as important as RAF Fylingdales is threatened by wildfire because it's literally in the middle of a moor, it's very vulnerable," she said. On Friday, Burnham said Britain was a "tinderbox" and outlined plans to expand support for fire services and ensure they are properly resourced. He said the UK must face up to the "changing climate" and transition to "more clean energy". His comments came ahead of the appointment of Baroness Blake of Leeds as fire minister. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "We're making almost Â£1.95bn available for fire services across England, and investing Â£97m for the biggest upgrade of national resilience capabilities in nearly twenty years. "We recognise that properties have been lost, firefighters have been hospitalised and people have been displaced, which is why we have also made available an emergency fund to support areas facing the greatest pressure." text: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged Twana Jamal Khdir appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday afternoon A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences. Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France. Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK. The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police. He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means. He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October. Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught. Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.
title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged

text: Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey The UK should join the EU's new Migration and Asylum Pact as a way of tackling small boat crossings across the Channel, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has said. The agreement, which came into force in June, aims to speed up the asylum process, increase the number of irregular migrants returned to their home countries and spread responsibility for asylum seekers across the EU. Sir Ed argues that signing up to the pact would allow the UK to return asylum seekers to the first EU country they entered, thereby "destroying the business model" of the gangs behind the crossings. Labour said the government's efforts to work with European countries to tackle small boat crossings were "bearing fruit". A Labour spokesperson said more than 47,000 crossings had been prevented in two years and 70,000 people with no right to be in the UK had been removed. "There's more to do and that will only happen by working in collaboration with the EU," the spokesperson added. So far this year, more than 14,000 people have arrived in the UK by small boat - a fall of 43% compared to the previous year. The EU's new pact, which was nearly 10 years in the making, introduces mandatory screening and an updated database to track those arriving in the bloc. Under the rules, EU nations must take in migrants from those member states that see the highest number of arrivals - such as Italy and Greece - or instead provide extra funding or resources. EU approves major overhaul of migration rules Inside secret police warehouse as Germany targets small boats gangs Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats Joining the agreement would require the UK to accept some asylum seekers from the EU. However, the Liberal Democrats argue numbers would be lower than those currently coming to the UK by small boat and that they would be screened before entering the country. The party says the scheme would save British taxpayers money, with the cost of participating - around Â£100m a year - amounting to a fraction of the Â£5bn spent on a "failing asylum system". Sir Ed said: "We have a plan that would finally end the small boats crisis: a pact with every EU country that will allow us to return people who come over the Channel, taking away the major pull factor that [Reform UK leader Nigel] Farage and co created and destroying the business model of the criminal gangs." Like the Liberal Democrats, some Labour politicians have made the argument that Brexit led to an increase in small boat crossings. Reform UK has previously dismissed such claims as "complete misinformation", arguing that EU membership "did nothing to make it easier to return asylum seekers". The EU pact replaces previous agreements - including the Dublin Regulation which allowed countries to return asylum seekers to the EU country they initially arrived in. But the protocol had been criticised for placing a disproportionate burden on countries receiving the bulk of the arrivals. The new so-called solidarity mechanism creates a pool of about 30,000 asylum seekers to be redistributed across the 27 member states. Instead of accepting asylum seekers, participating countries could instead choose to pay â¬20,000 (Â£17,000) per person not taken. Arrivals must be registered, with identity checks to prevent those who pose security or public health risks from entering the EU undetected. People aged six and above would have their biometric data collected, with information - such as fingerprints - stored on the Eurodac database. The UK government has previously said it would like to regain access to the database, something it lost following Brexit. Joining the pact could prove tricky for the UK and would require unanimous approval from all EU states. The government would also have to pass new laws to implement the pact and could have to standardise its procedures with the EU bloc. Between 1 January and 19 August 2026, a total of 15,897 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 42% of asylum applications between April 2025 to March 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 20 August 2025 to 19 August 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to âsmash the gangsâ behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from April 2025 to March 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,000 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,535 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from April 2025 to March 2026. This was down by 22% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. title: Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey

text: Burnham unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas A rough sleeper lies on a pavement in London last month Every rough sleeper in England will be offered accommodation this winter, the prime minister has said. Andy Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July and now says he wants "to get everyone in for Christmas". Emergency accommodation will be provided to end the need for rough sleeping alongside practical support for any health needs, as part of a Â£442m package. Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said Burnham promised to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester when mayor of the area but "failed because he didn't do the hard work necessary". Burnham's pledge seeks to build on the success of Everyone In, a Covid pandemic-era scheme that saw thousands of rough sleepers housed in hotels and temporary accommodation. About 37,000 people were helped by that scheme, following its launch in March 2020. The charity Shelter found that about a quarter of them had found settled accommodation, in the form of housing lasting at least six months. , external The PM's announcement comes with an additional Â£102m in new funding, taking Burnham's total commitment to tackling rough sleeping to Â£442m since becoming prime minister. The money is said to be "fully funded" within the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. As well as providing immediate support to get people off the streets, the funding is also designed to deliver more than 1,000 homes over the next three years to provide rough sleepers with permanent accommodation. The funding will also provide "intensive wraparound support", typically psychiatric and drug and alcohol services to help people rebuild their lives. Burnham said he did not believe "anybody should be forced to sleep rough". He added: "And actually when you do leave people sleeping rough it can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, in and out of hospital beds and sometimes in contact with the police." The prime minister said the government funding "may not fully get us there" as he appealed to charities and faith organisations to help ensure an offer is made to everybody who needs it. He added: "We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again." Rooms in shared flats or houses, B&B accommodation, warm spaces for short-term refuge and supported lodgings are among the types of accommodation mentioned in the government's guidance that could be used to bring people in off the streets. Burnham also told The Big Issue , external he would commit to donating 15% of his prime minister's salary to tackle homelessness, which follows his decision to give 15% of his MP salary to causes in his Makerfield constituency. A prime minister is entitled to an additional salary of Â£83,837 on top of their salary for being an MP. Recent PMs have claimed Â£75,440, with the previous government of Sir Keir Starmer continuing the freeze on ministerial salaries. For the Conservatives, Sir James said the PM's pledge lacked a plan for delivery. He said: "As with many of his other commitments, there is very little detail on how this one will be paid for." The previous Conservative government had pledged to end rough sleeping by 2024. According to official data, there were an estimated 4,793 people sleeping rough on a single night in England in the autumn of 2025 , external , a 96% increase in five years. Rough sleeping is the most visible form of homelessness, and does not include people staying in temporary accommodation like hostels, or sofa surfing. However, the annual snapshot is seen as significantly undercounting the extent of the problem due to strict rules over how the data is collected. Liberal Democrat housing spokesperson Gideon Amos said "sticking plasters won't fix the homelessness crisis", adding a "proper long-term plan" is needed to prevent people finding themselves "back on the streets once the festive headlines fade". He urged Burnham to commit to a Lib Dem target to build 150,000 social homes every year. Deputy Reform UK leader Richard Tice also criticised Burnham's efforts to tackle homelessness while Greater Manchester mayor. He described the government's new plans as "yet another vague announcement with no substances which uses our most vulnerable for political point-scoring". The Bed Every Night scheme which Burnham set up while mayor now provides more than 600 beds a night for people who might otherwise be on the streets. Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester by 2020 when he became mayor. There were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester in 2017 when he was elected, according to government figures. By 2020 - at the time of the Covid pandemic - that figure had more than halved to 125, so Burnham missed his target. It fell further to 90 in 2021; however the latest data showed it had risen to 197 by 2025. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, challenged about the recent year-on-year increase in rough sleeping in Greater Manchester, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the lack of a national programme meant "everybody knew that Greater Manchester was the place where you got the support". Rough sleeping has increased nationally in recent years. In autumn 2025, the number of people estimated to be sleeping rough on a single night in England was 4,793 - a record high. However the annual rate of rough sleeping in Greater Manchester per 100,000 people has been lower than the average for England in recent years. Jasmine Basran, head of policy at Crisis, said the homeless charity welcomed the announcement and believed an end to rough sleeping was possible. She urged departments across government to work together to address the issue - saying too many people being discharged from hospital or leaving care were ending up on the streets. Sarah Elliott, Shelter's chief executive, called Burnham's pledge a "game-changing move". She said "tackling the most visible form of homelessness is a strong start" but urged the prime minister to act on his promise to build more council houses to help people living in temporary accommodation. Chloe used to sleep rough and says she welcomes the initiative Chloe, 27, from London, ended up rough sleeping last year after spending time in contact with care and foster services growing up. She slept in parks away from the centre of the city to try and to stay hidden, and says no rough sleeper would turn down a bed if it came with the right support. Chloe was helped by Crisis who housed her in temporary accommodation and now has a place to study at film school. She still thinks that the scheme will be welcomed by the majority of rough sleepers. She said: "In general, people on the street want a home. People usually end up coming back to homelessness for mental health or financial reasons. "So if that could also be addressed, there is no person sleeping on the street right now who wouldn't want some type of security." Meron, who is originally from Eritrea, has been sleeping in a tent in a tunnel in central London for about two months. He says he became homeless after his three-month contract at an Amazon Warehouse ended. "People leave their rubbish out. There are cars, loud music, it's not dangerous but I can't sleep. I keep applying for jobs but I can't find one." title: Burnham unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas

text: Burnham received £345,000 of donations ahead of becoming PM Andy Burnham has registered accepting Â£345,000 of donations over the past year including Â£164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury. The donations, listed in the most recent version of the MPs' register of interests, , external are the prime minister's first declarations since he was elected to Parliament in June. Separately, Burnham has also listed hospitality and gifts he received in the year before he returned to Parliament, including trips to Glastonbury, Lancashire Cricket Club and the Aintree Racecourse. A Labour Party spokesperson said: "It's right that political campaigns are funded by the generous support of party donors, rather than via the public purse. "All declarations have been made in line with Parliamentary and Electoral Commission rules." New MPs are required to register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election. Lord Sainsbury's donations went towards Burnham's campaign to become Labour leader. Businessman Gary Lubner and former Greater Manchester night-time economy tsar Sacha Lord donated Â£25,000 and Â£35,000 to the campaign respectively. The TV production company Charlie Parsons Creative contributed Â£50,000 and the think tank ThinkLabour, formerly known as Labour Together, provided Â£22,186. The donations included the provision of office space, IT equipment, staffing, polling, travel, social media support and message testing. Burnham's list also includes Â£20,000 of donations towards mayoral campaigning  from the trade unions Unison, the Communications Workers Union and the Fire Brigades Union. Labour peer Lord Blunkett appears on the list having donated Â£2,000 towards Burnham's campaign to become the MP for Makerfield. Gifts and hospitality Burnham accepted when he was mayor of Greater Manchester include: Four tickets to Glastonbury, where he was speaking at an event, from the festival organisers and Â£1,000 for accommodation from the music industry organisation PRS for Music Tickets worth Â£3,800 to the Brit Awards in Manchester from Sony Music Entertainment Two tickets worth Â£500 for the Aintree Racecourse from the Jockey Club Racecourse Two tickets, valued at Â£458, from Lancashire Cricket Club for a game in The Hundred tournament A hamper basket and Wedgewood tea set worth Â£340 from the ambassador of Qatar Shortly after becoming prime minister in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer became embroiled in a row over the gifts he had accepted including tickets to a Taylor Swift concert and thousands of pounds for clothes. He subsequently paid back more than Â£6,000 worth of gifts and hospitality. He also tightened the rules so that serving ministers had to consider "the need to maintain the public's confidence in the standard of propriety" when accepting gifts. Clarification 20 August: This article was amended to describe PRS for Music as a music industry organisation rather than a campaign group.
title: Burnham received £345,000 of donations ahead of becoming PM

text: Suspended Reform UK member vows to fight to remain in party This video can not be played 'I'm going to fight,' says suspended Reform UK member Tim Montgomerie Political commentator Tim Montgomerie has told BBC Newsnight he will fight his suspension from Reform UK for criticising senior party figures in media interviews. He said his appeal against suspension would be a test case of whether Reform could tolerate free speech. The party said Montgomerie had been suspended in line with its rules after public criticism he made. Montgomerie is a right-of-centre political commentator who defected from the Conservatives to Reform UK in 2024,  and who has seen himself as a critical friend of the party leadership. But it seems he is now regarded as more of a critic and less of a friend - and has had  his party membership suspended. On Friday, Montgomerie had told the BBC he was frustrated by party leader Nigel Farage's "aggrieved tone" after last week's Clacton by-election. And on a Spectator podcast on Tuesday, he had said another senior party figure, Zia Yusuf, needed to become a team player and should not act "like a child" in politics. It is understood his suspension came after the podcast was recorded but before it was released. "I am going to fight this suspension. I want to stay in Reform. I didn't leave the Conservative Party lightly," he told Newsnight. "I think Reform can reach parts of the country that the Conservative Party never will be able to so I'm going to fight my corner in Reform and I'm going to make this a test case of whether it is a party that can tolerate free speech and dissent," he added. Montgomerie said he supported Reform's policies on immigration and welfare, but he has also highlighted internal tensions in the party. In a video statement on X after news of his suspension emerged on the Guido Fawkes website, Montgomerie said he was only trying to make the party "better and stronger" with his public criticisms. He added that Farage did not know about the decision to suspend him, and he had warned the Reform leader when he joined the party that he would be critical at times, as he had been of the Tory leadership when he ran the ConservativeHome website. Reform's leadership will have to decide whether it is more politically difficult to rescind rather than to retain Montgomerie's party membership. title: Suspended Reform UK member vows to fight to remain in party

text: UK 'supports Ukraine 100%', Burnham says, after Russia's drone warning Ukraine has in recent weeks hit a number of logistics hubs belonging to online retailer Wildberries UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said London will continue "to support Ukraine 100%", after Moscow warned of "consequences" following confirmation that British-made drones were used in recent Ukrainian strikes in Russia. "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change," he said. The Russian embassy in the UK earlier accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay". Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the largest online retailer Wildberries. Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained that the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me". This video can not be played Prime Minister Andy Burnham: "We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need" This is not the first time that Russia has warned the UK over its role in providing Ukraine with drone technology and Storm Shadow missiles . The Russian embassy said "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer", but did not elaborate on the type of threat Moscow was considering. The latest phase of the war has directly affected Russia's domestic fuel supplies and dented the Russian economy. The UK has been one of Ukraine's biggest international supporters since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Ministry of Defence said the UK was "committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's illegal invasion". Two British companies are known to have built drones supplied to Kyiv . A military source confirmed to the BBC that UK drones had been used in recent attacks on Russia that reportedly caused more than Â£35bn in economic damage. The Kremlin has regularly singled out the UK - along with the US - for its role in arming and backing Kyiv politically and financially since the start of the war. It was London - then under Boris Johnson's leadership - that supplied Ukraine with very effective anti-tank weapons that helped to stop Moscow's advance on Kyiv in the first few weeks of the war. The UK has since provided more modern weaponry and has also been actively training Ukrainian soldiers. In July, Burnham showed that Britain's support would continue by making his first international visit as prime minister to Kyiv. On Russia's state TV channels, the anti-UK rhetoric has intensified in recent weeks, with invited experts and lawmakers regularly calling for strikes against the UK. Russia currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory but its forces have had very little success on the front line for months. Nevertheless, casualties have continued to mount. UN officials say last month's civilian death toll of 437 people in Ukraine was the highest since May 2022. In Russia, a foreign ministry spokesman told the Tass news agency on Tuesday that in the past week 69 people including three children had been killed. In the latest Russian attacks on Ukraine, 17 people were killed, including 10 in the village of Pechenihy in north-eastern Ukraine early on Tuesday. Private homes, a cafe and post office were hit, as two missiles claimed the lives of 10 villagers. Elsewhere, three Ukrainians died in Sumy, two in Zaporizhzhia and two in Kherson. Moscow's warning to the UK comes after a wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russia. Five people were killed in a residential area of Rostov region in the south of the country at the weekend. Hundreds of drones have been launched by Ukrainian forces towards the Moscow region in the past two days alone. Regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said on Tuesday that a 10-year-old girl was hurt and a Wildberries warehouse was damaged. As well as deploying imported drones, Ukraine has been able to use home-grown drone and missile technology in recent weeks, including its FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. In a separate development on Tuesday, the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA, said it had been informed that "a drone exploded at a bus stop used by staff" travelling to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in the Russian-occupied southern Ukraine. The IAEA said it had been told by the Moscow-installed plant director that one person was killed and another three seriously injured. It did not say who carried out the attack. "No nuclear safety or security damage was reported," the watchdog added. Two Russian missiles killed 10 people early on Tuesday in the centre of the village of Pechenihy, officials said Monday night saw heavy Ukrainian strikes, with Russian officials reporting that some 620 drones had been flown towards the region surrounding Moscow. Russian air defences destroyed more than 180 of them, but several people were wounded, the officials added. On Saturday night, Ukraine fired some 822 drones towards Russia, with 600 aiming for Moscow, according to its regional governor, who said the Russian capital had suffered "one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory" . Seven deaths were reported across Russia. UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia Russia and Ukraine trade more deadly strikes How Ukraine is taking the war 'deeper' into Russia Much of the focus on Russian threats towards Ukraine's Western allies has been on hybrid warfare. Although incidents are rarely confirmed as Russian-sponsored, numerous cases have been reported around Europe involving drones flying close to sensitive military and industrial sites. Last week, German officials warned of a "real, very acute" risk from hybrid attacks after a drone loaded with explosives was defused close to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport, which acts as a military hub for Germany and its Nato allies. The German government is planning to hand its BND and BfV spy agencies sweeping new powers to counter drone threats and hack and disrupt hostile actors.
title: UK 'supports Ukraine 100%', Burnham says, after Russia's drone warning

text: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal". It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election. This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years". More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. The government has spent the last few weeks recruiting producers, videographers and strategists, working out of both Whitehall and No 10 North in Manchester. In his first month as PM, Burnham posted more than 50 times on Instagram, ranging from meetings with world leaders, campaigners, farmers and influencers, to meme-based content like ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey as part of an announcement on business rates. Strategists believe Instagram and TikTok can play to Burnham's communication strengths and sense of humour. The PM's social media game has been a hit with pundits They're all at it, of course. Videos of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch tearing into the budget or mocking ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer have gone viral. Reform UK's Nigel Farage has by far the biggest online audience of any UK party leader, with 7.6 million followers across Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube. In Scotland, the SNP have long mobilised their online army to campaign for independence, building a following larger than that of the Lib Dems, which campaigns across Britain, whose leader Ed Davey has achieved some success with campaign stunts going viral. Restore Britain, founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe, enjoys its highest level of support among users of X. The platform is owned by Elon Musk who has publicly endorsed the party, expanding its reach. Plaid Cymru, newly installed in government in Wales, is still experimenting with its approach, using First Minister Rhun Ap Iorweth in "fun" memes while also posting more serious interview excerpts. The Greens' Zack Polanski has made much of running his own accounts, though as he has found in recent weeks, this comes with risks too. So how much is enough? In a world where reputations can be made (or broken) with one comment or collaboration, getting the balance right is tricky â being accessible, authentic and approachable, without being cringe. And does it make any difference to elections? Cameron's successor, Theresa May, was similarly doubtful about the merits of social media. When she took office she rebuffed aides who suggested she start tweeting: "People don't say 'pass me the hashtag newspaper, or I'd like a hashtag coffee'." Announcements were to be made formally. When cabinet ministers were appointed in May's first reshuffle, it was heralded in press statements beneath the UK government coat of arms. By contrast, this summer, presenting my 5 Live show from Downing Street during Burnham's first reshuffle, I could predict the appearance of another new minister because the two-person social media team from No 10 would move into position to capture the new arrivals on their cameras. Of course, prime ministers (and wannabes) have long adapted to new technology. Winston Churchill harnessed the power of radio, but thought television a vulgar diversion. In the 1960s, Labour's Harold Wilson modelled his TV campaigning on JFK in America. In the 1990s, and 2000s leaders like Tony Blair were just as likely to be found on the chatshow sofa as on the Today programme. Nigel Farage's social media following is larger than that of any other UK leader Now, podcasts give long-form - and less combative - opportunities to connect with voters, while social media gives a quick hit of direct democratic dopamine. Peter Hyman, a former adviser to both Tony Blair and Keir Starmer when in Downing Street, said the success of Burnham's early digital output was about "quantity as well as quality". "You have to narrate the story of what you are doing three or four or five times a day so that you are out there regularly," Hyman said. "Keir Starmer wasn't out there enough and therefore it wasn't landing." There is a causality dilemma here. Is Burnham more popular in the polls because he is racking up the likes on social media, or is he doing better online because people like him? Not everyone is convinced. Cody Dahler, a comedian who posts sweary political explainers to his two million followers, warns voters will become cynical if they sense politicians are just using social media simply "as a comms tool". Burnham, Dahler told me on Newsnight, comes across like a "cool substitute teacher". And after Burnham released a video discussing what a bread roll is called in different parts of the country â barm, cob or bap - to promote his plans for devolution, broadcaster Piers Morgan asked him to "stop wasting your time and ours with these cringe videos". And therein lies the difficulty of striking a balance. Bea Timpson, a former press secretary to Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak who says she prefers "trad media" like broadcast and print, added: â"I have to accept that it's now non-negotiable to be online a bit, but you definitely can be too much." TV and online websites remain the most used sources for news, but more and more of us say we also get news from social media, according to media watchdog Ofcom. While this is highest among 16-24 year olds at 78%, a majority of adults in every age group use social media to access news, apart from the over-65s. Even among over 75s, 22% find out what is happening in the world from social media. For politicians, this is no longer just about reaching young people â this is all voters. Some platforms are more important than others. Even after Elon Musk's conversion of Twitter into X, you will still see MPs, spin doctors and journalists in the Westminster village scrolling through the platform, but digital strategists say "real voters" are found on other platforms. The main parties have far more followers on Facebook (four million combined), which is much more widely used overall, than X (where they have a combined 3.2 million). Politicians have always looked abroad for policy and campaigning ideas, and social media is no different. Those on the right seek to emulate the impact Donald Trump has on TruthSocial, while left-wing politicians look to the success of Zohran Mamdani becoming mayor of New York. Some have even imported social media experts from overseas. In 2019 Boris Johnson hired New Zealand duo Ben Guerin and Sean Topham to run the digital campaign for the general election. They imported into UK politics the concept of "shitposting", releasing deliberately bad images in order to generate a reaction. This included posting a tweet featuring the slogan "Get Brexit Done" in Comic Sans, a font loathed by graphic designers. There was a method in the madness. "People are more likely to engage with something if they feel like it's been written by a human, not by a committee of design experts," Guerin told me. "It's pretty easy to go viral for doing something weird and wacky, but that doesn't always advance the objectives of your campaign." This seems to be borne out by some recent hits. Burnham's TikTok post rating pub snacks attracted a million views. Yet a less gimmicky video, straightforwardly listing the five things he said he had done in his first week as PM, got five million. There is an inherent tension in political social media. Authenticity is key. Yet who really expects the prime minister to be shooting and uploading his own content? Back in 2013 I wrote a story about how Cameron's Twitter account had favourited a tweet mocking William Hague from an account handle that made a crude joke about former Tory MP Norman Tebbit being injured in the Brighton bombing. The prime minister's director of communications called me to complain about my "slapdash and crappy" reporting. My crime? Including a sentence which allowed for the possibility that someone other than Cameron had clicked on the like button by mistake. This would, apparently, spoil the magic for those that thought the prime minister was running his own account for his 500,000 followers. Zack Polanski has faced criticism for a controversial post and collaboration We now know that Zack Polanski does indeed have his own log-ins. The leader of the Green Party in England and Wales faced criticism in May for sharing a post condemning police actions in the Golders Green attack, for which he apologised. Then in July he accepted an Instagram collaboration which included a man wearing a T-shirt featuring a cartoon guillotine and the song lyrics "we're only making plans for Nigel". Reform UK said it amounted to incitement of violence against Farage. "I'm accepting my responsibility in that I shouldn't have accepted that collaboration," Polanski said, but refused to apologise. Reform UK's Gawain Towler, a long-time media adviser to Nigel Farage, says: "âMy big takeaway is: don't be a berk on social media, âwhich I think was Zack Polanski's big takeaway too." Kemi Badenoch's performances at Prime Minister's Questions have gone viral Dov Forman, who helped Tory-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick grow his following from 20,000 to more than half a million with viral clips including confronting fare dodgers on the London Underground, says it is "risky" for a leader to run their own social media. But sometimes it can be a risk worth taking. Badenoch has taken to directing her own videos, telling aides what she wants to post. She has attracted backing on X from American rappers Nicki Minaj and Azealia Banks. Those are the sort of authentic third-party endorsements politicians crave. On the day he became prime minister, a video was released of Burnham being interviewed on the Career Ladder, a series run by Ukrainian TikToker Max Klymenko who interviews guests about their career, while standing on a ladder. "If they personally haven't seen the channel it's sometimes quite difficult to make sense for them," Klymenko says. Burnham had seen the show, and did use the ladder. Which leads us to the big question: Does any of this actually work? Emma Connolly, an academic who has researched this at the Digital Speech Lab at UCL, isn't sure. "We don't necessarily have really strong evidence or convincing evidence that it could really persuade or transform the opinion of opponent voters or even those that are undecided," she says. Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence? Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise And this in turn raises the question of how long the Burnham digital honeymoon might last. Can a prime minister TikTok his way through a war, terror attack or controversial court case? Announcing a new giveaway may go viral, but what about the details of the cuts to pay for it? The truth is none of this is new, as Hyman explains: "The politicians who get this wrong think that social media is now the only place to be, and a substitute for doing the hard work and the heavy lifting of actually getting the right policy, getting the right narrative, and telling that story properly," he says. "Politics is about winning arguments." After all, politicians have always wanted to be liked. It's just these days they can see it instantly if you hit that heart button on your feed. title: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough

text: How one man gets new laws passed - again and again Ron Bailey has been called many things in his 40 years of political campaigning, not all of them printable. "The UK's most successful parliamentary campaigner," by a former Friends of the Earth director. "The most effective and relentless lobbyist that it has been my misfortune to encounter during the last two decades," according to ex-minister Sir Oliver Letwin. "A bit of a pain in the arse at times," by Lib Dem peer (and friend) Lord Foster. Over the years Bailey has worked for groups including the Green Party, the Community Rights Project and the Sustainable Energy Association. In that time he estimates he has been involved in getting 16 bills into law and has had a hand in a further 25 law changes. Surprising stats for someone who used to have a poster that read "Don't vote, it only encourages them". In his younger days Bailey was less interested in parliamentary process, preferring direct action. His folk-singer brother first awakened his interest in politics while being "asked to leave" grammar school for "messing about" deepened his dislike of authority. He cut his campaigning teeth in the 1960s, joining protests against harsh homelessness laws that split up families and getting involved in the squatting movement. Activities included occupying hostels, moving homeless families into empty houses, and battling with bailiffs. The campaigns were infused with the revolutionary spirit of the time but underpinned by Bailey's forensic understanding of the law. He recalls spending hours in the British Library researching property laws going back to the 14th Century, so that when challenged he was armed with the facts. One of Bailey's first campaigns was fighting for homeless families at the King Hill hostel in Kent, who had been forcibly separated More than a decade later, Bailey began trying to change the law, rather than just reading about it. One of his early victories was a freedom of information campaign. In 1983, the Greater London Council Grants Committee awarded one of his projects enough money to rent an office and employ staff. Happy to bite the hand that feeds, Bailey used the cash to launch a campaign demanding that they make their meetings public. Next, he pushed for a Local Government (Access to Information) Bill, which expanded the public's access to council meetings and documents. To build support for the bill, Bailey and his team contacted hundreds of local groups sending them the "secret files" which detailed activities councils were getting up to behind closed doors. One of Bailey's favourite examples, he recalls, was a council that voted for a motion supporting freedom of information - in private. He knew the campaign was paying off when he overheard MPs in a parliamentary bar complaining about the flood of letters they were receiving on the subject. "I don't call myself a lobbyist," Bailey says. "I call myself a community mobiliser. That's what's crucial. You don't win these campaigns in Parliament, you win them outside Parliament." The then Conservative government had a big majority and had opposed the bill, but in the face of public pressure, relented. Bailey says he and his team were careful to allow ministers to "save face", altering the wording of their proposal so the government didn't look like it had climbed down. In 1974 Bailey was one of the organisers behind the occupation of the Centrepoint building in London, as part of a protest against homelessness. Last year, he told the BBC he spent four months "meticulously planning" the action. "Giving your opponent a way out" is one of his golden rules of campaigning - his full list can be found in his new book Institutionalised Deceit: Taking the Lid off Westminster Governance. Another is to avoid party tribalism. Despite voting Green, Bailey has rarely been picky about who he works with. In the 1980s, he teamed up with the Association for the Conservation of Energy, a body governed by directors and CEOs. In a goodbye speech at the end of his time with them, Bailey said: "Perhaps we have both learnt something. "I have learnt that not all capitalist bastards are capitalist bastards and you have learnt that not all anarchist nutters are anarchist nutters." Another mantra is to always appear "ultra reasonable". In his book he writes: "Make it as difficult as possible for people to oppose you." Among his success, he counts: the Home Energy Conservation Act, which put a duty on councils to set out how they were improving home energy efficiency the Private Hire Vehicles Act, which regulated minicabs the Road Traffic Reduction Act, which required local councils to produce traffic reduction plans One of Bailey's key methods of getting laws passed is the private members' bills process - the parliamentary procedure which begins with the deputy speaker, wearing white gloves and picking small numbered balls out of a goldfish bowl. The lucky MPs, whose numbers are drawn, get crucial parliamentary time to introduce their own bill. As soon as the numbers were drawn, Bailey would move fast - immediately lobbying the seven MPs on the list, presenting them with bills, oven-ready for presentation. He became a master of the tricky process of turning private members' bills into law. That put him on a collision course with Conservative MP Eric Forth. Forth was a dedicated parliamentarian and one of the most vehement opponents of the private members' bill process. He would regularly try to block bills by talking them out. The Bromley and Chiselhurst MP argued that such bills represented the "dreams of this or that group and the proper aspirations of good minded-people" but were "not necessarily very well-thought through". Forth was so prolific at "filibustering" backbenchers bills that the Friday sessions in the House of Commons, where the bills are debated, gained the nickname "Eric Forth's killing fields". In his book, Bailey described Forth as "uncrackable" - but he was able to claim victories against the MP. In an (ultimately successful) effort to save his Private Hire Vehicles Bill, Bailey organised an intense local campaign, which saw leaflets sent to every one of Forth's 50,000 constituents. Bailey was also not above returning to the direct action tactics of his youth. He once locked the Liberal Democrat chief whip in his office, in a bid to prevent him from being lobbied by rival campaigners. Now in his 80s, Bailey is recovering from his sixth stroke, while insomnia and restless leg syndrome keep him up at night. But his friend Lib Dem peer Lord Don Foster says he is "still at it". "Still chasing, still writing parliamentary questions. "Above everything, Ron Bailey has probably got more pieces of legislation through Parliament than the vast majority of cabinet ministers." title: How one man gets new laws passed - again and again

text: Meet the men applying for the 'hardest job in British politics' Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are squaring off in the Scottish Labour leadership contest Wanted: one leader for Scottish Labour. Must enjoy long hours, complex trade-offs and difficult questions. That may not be the official job description for Scottish Labour leader, but it's perhaps not far from the truth. After all, Anas Sarwar described this gig as "the hardest job in British politics". Despite this health warning, two candidates are on the ballot paper vying to take on the challenge - Michael Marra and Joe Fagan. I sat down with both of them for the Scotcast podcast to learn a bit about who they are, where they think Labour has gone wrong, and their prescription for fixing things. Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions Lennon criticises 'nasty' Scottish Labour as leadership bid fails But before we got into the nitty gritty of politics, I wanted to know a bit more about these two candidates. We started with an ice-breaker: If they had to give a Ted Talk (an online lecture about a topic they're passionate about), what would their subject be? For Michael Marra, it was his beloved football team, Dundee United. Given they've just endured back-to-back 4-0 defeats, there's a joke here about the North East Labour MSP backing lost causes. Joe Fagan opted for a lecture on Cold War Berlin. And there was even a comparison about the "eerie resemblance" between Stasi HQ in East Germany and the office he occupied when he was the leader of South Lanarkshire Council. This video can not be played Labour leadership: Marra says party must work for Scotland But we weren't here to talk about DUFC's glory days or the fall of the wall. This was a conversation about everything that's been going on with Scottish Labour. The most newsworthy reflection probably came from Fagan, the South of Scotland MSP, who was critical of Sarwar's decision to leave Holyrood and take a place in the House of Lords. He wished Sarwar well on a personal level, but said it "wasn't a good look" for him to stop being a Glasgow MSP and head to Westminster's upper chamber. Fagan said that he would never personally take a seat in the Lords. And not just because he thinks the robes look "ridiculous". But he did concede that it would be difficult to turn down the offer of a ministerial post from the prime minister. Anas Sarwar accepted a peerage after stepping down as Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra also had some criticisms of Anas Sarwar's approach as leader. He praised his work ethic and communication abilities, but said that the party had been too focused on Sarwar in the last five years. Privately other party figures have said that same â that the party's style was too "presidential" in recent years, rather than showcasing a team of spokespeople. Marra told me the party had "lost definition as to who the Labour Party is" and had become "too narrow in our leadership and the circle of influence around the leader". A big question hanging over these interviews was what will the approach of these candidates be to independence? While Scottish Labour isn't going to support that sort of constitutional change any time soon (or perhaps ever), there are voices inside the party who argue it's time to engage with the debate around the grounds for a second referendum. But both Michael Marra and Joe Fagan don't have much time for this argument. Fagan said it would be "obvious" when the will of the Scottish people had changed, but we weren't at that point. He insisted that debates around the process for independence was a relic of the "Sturgeon era", and that that period was now "history". Marra told me he wasn't clear how a trigger for a second referendum would work, arguing that people are more concerned with issues like the cost of living and the NHS. Labour leadership: Fagan says indyref calls and Sturgeon era 'over' This leadership contest has â somewhat unexpectedly â focussed on the issue of gender in recent days. When Glasgow MSP Monica Lennon failed to make the ballot , she released an explosive statement suggesting the other two had been "punching down on trans people". Both Marra and Fagan have rejected that accusation. But they both have strong views on the issue of gender reform. Remember, MSPs passed a bill in 2022 that would have made it easier for someone to change their legally recognised sex â so-called "self-ID". It was ultimately blocked by the UK government, a decision upheld in the courts. Labour MSPs at the time were whipped to support it. Some gave up their spokesperson positions in order to vote against. Marra came to a deal with Sarwar â he was allowed to abstain. But he told Scotcast he felt so strongly about the issue that he would've been willing to resign over it. Monica Lennon did not secure the nominations required to make the leadership ballot Fagan wasn't in Holyrood at the time, but his view watching from outside was that Labour MSPs shouldn't have backed it. When it came to the economic side of Scottish politics, both candidates expressed the view that some Scots â especially middle earners â are paying too much tax. But that doesn't necessarily mean cuts across the board. Fagan argued that there's a case for "widening" the tax base through some new approaches, such as environmental taxes. And Marra â whose professional background is in economics â said that he was willing to consider looking at a wealth tax. And when it comes to oil and gas both wannabee leaders think the UK government should go ahead with extracting at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields. Scotcast - The Scottish Labour leadership interviews Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are vying to succeed Anas Sarwar as Scottish Labour leader.  They talk to us about their partyâs failures, the route to indyref2 and guilty pleasures. Some in Labour were unhappy when Lennon didn't make the ballot for this contesting, lamenting a lack of breadth in the contest. And they maybe have a point. It doesn't feel like Scottish Labour members are choosing between two radically different candidates here. This pair broadly agree on a lot. That being said, both Marra and Fagan seem thoughtful, eloquent and capable politicians. But the trajectory of Scottish Labour's Holyrood results make for grim reading â they've lost MSPs at every election since 1999. A once mighty political force in Scotland has just 17 MSPs now. It's a movement that requires a massive shot of adrenaline. It needs something that can win back its once natural voters, who seem to have found political homes elsewhere. It doesn't feel like either Fagan or Marra have outlined that recovery plan yet. And, to be fair, they have a bit of time until they face the public again. But they will need to outline that grand idea at some point. Or the winner risks simply being the latest captain of a political ship that's sinking in the rough seas of Scottish politics.
