text: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options? Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants major reform of the social care system in England, calling the current situation "bad for everybody". In a speech at a care home on Wednesday he announced that cross-party talks involving the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats would start later. Burnham also said he had asked Baroness Casey - who is carrying out a review of social care - to bring forward her report by a year. She will now set out her recommendations in 2027. He confirmed that her review will also look at the question of how to pay for any reforms. BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching reform and how much they could cost. Some people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life. It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than Â£100,000. One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold. In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of Â£35,000. Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between Â£1.3bn and Â£2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population. The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations. But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances. In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care. This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes. It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan. The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped. In England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than Â£23,250. This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings. Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support. Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to Â£100,000. The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been Â£1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified. The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down. An alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use. This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home. Scotland has implemented such a system. However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet. But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing. The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost Â£7.5bn a year by 2036. Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay. Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers. Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses. Some have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS. This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria. The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around Â£19bn a year extra by 2036. When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service. It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died. But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further. In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded. And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028. It's worth bearing in mind that these four approaches above are not mutually exclusive. Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.
title: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?

text: 'Every day I'm just winging it': The families hoping for social care reform Emma Riley is a dental nurse from Manchester, as was her mother Carol before she retired Andy Burnham has pledged to reform the adult social care system in England, meeting the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to try to find "common ground" on the issue. He wants an independent review of care to be brought forward by a year to 2027, as well as major reforms to pay and conditions for staff and the creation of a national care service. But the prime minister said "difficult decisions" would have to be made on tax to fund sustainable change, adding that in an "ideal world" no-one should have to sell their home to pay for care. BBC Your Voice has been speaking to families affected by what they see as shortfalls in the system. Emma Riley has been caring for her mother Carol, who has dementia, since she lost her father 18 months ago. "She's a cracking lady, still with a sense of humour but she's living with this awful condition," said Riley, from Manchester. She is paying Â£34 an hour for a care company to come to the house three times a week, which she describes as a "huge chunk of money" although she is happy with the level of care. Riley wants to keep her mum in the family home, but the caring commitments affect her job as a dental nurse. She started applying to the local council for funding to support her mother at home at the beginning of the year, but six months on, she is still waiting for a final decision. "It's not the social worker's fault, it is just the caseload," she said. Riley called for more communication to help her navigate the system, adding: "I'm blindly going through it at the moment. "Every day I'm just winging it but there's a human being upstairs." Riley said she heard the prime minister's speech and it had left her feeling "quietly confident". Burnham has announced that a review of social care by veteran Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey would now be published next summer. "I do think Baroness Casey will make the changes we need," Riley added. Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care The Greenwood family in West Yorkshire say they have had to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for their mother, Mavis Lisa Greenwood, from Halifax, West Yorkshire, said she would be supportive of the prime minister if he managed to change how the care sector operates. "It does need changing and hopefully it will get better," she said. Greenwood said her family is having to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for her mother, Mavis, who is 90 and in local respite care. It is costing Â£1,305 a week, something Greenwood says the family "cannot sustain". She said they now face the prospect of having to sell her mother's home, describing this as "very distressing". Greenwood backs Burnham's proposal to increase pay in the sector and suggests it will help attract more staff. "Carers do need to be paid more," she said. "There are some fantastic people doing the job on little wages." Greenwood told the BBC's Your Voice that both her parents had worked "all their lives saving for the future". "Yet here we are in a situation of stress not knowing how we are going to continue with mum in the home," she added. "We can't give up our jobs, we need to work to pay our bills." Sophie and her father Stephen, who died in 2024 when she was just 16 Sophie Daniels was 16 when her father died in 2024 as a result of stage 4 glioblastoma, a highly aggressive brain tumour. The 18-year-old felt that there was a lack of support for her family. Along with her mother and sister, she looked after her father at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, as "social care provision was incredibly limited". Daniels said: "We hardly had any help and we were left to figure things out ourselves. "Thankfully, charities helped us with that but towards the end my mum had to give up work to care for my dad." She said that one of the biggest practical challenges her family faced was a lack of a lifting service to help him move around the house. "He fell fairly frequently and a lack of lifting service meant that our dad was forced to either wait for hours on the floor for an ambulance or for us to try and use techniques to pull my dad up." Andy Burnham made his speech at a north London care home, where he spoke to some of the residents Steve West, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, cared for his mother for many years before taking the difficult decision to place her in a care home. She died earlier this year. West, 64, said he was "frustrated hearing the same issues that need fixing being discussed by each new government". Listening to the prime minister's speech, he said that a proposed national care service "could give focus, but its remit needs to be confirmed". "I think a cross-party approach would be a benefit as the plans would take a few terms of parliament at least and then to maintain the benefits for years to come," he added. He said when caring for his mother, the biggest challenge was "knowing who to speak to" and "dealing with several health bodies", sometimes having to repeat her medical history several times. "She got progressively worse and I remember one time sitting in a car park for an hour-and-a-half trying to get an emergency social worker," he said, adding that "having a system that is unified would be a massive help". West believes the prime minister "needs to focus on one or two big-ticket items - those that will have the biggest impact". He said if relatives caring for loved ones were paid at similar rates to private companies, "perhaps more people would feel they were able to provide support" as they would not be negatively impacted by cutting work hours or leaving their jobs. John Barry was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died from the disease in 2024. Pictured here with his wife Jeanette. Jeanette Barry from Essex was married to her husband John for 42 years before he was diagnosed with dementia in 2018. The former policeman was moved to a local care home as his needs became more complex. "At one point he was roaming the streets at night because he thought he was still on duty," said Barry. "I couldn't keep him in the house, so at 2am or 3am I was having to follow him to make sure he was alright." She paid Â£2,000 a month in care home fees out of her husband's police pension, on top of local authority funding, although she didn't "begrudge a penny of that money" as he was well looked after. She says she was told by one social worker that she would have to remortgage her house or her husband would be moved to another care home, but he was later reassessed and qualified for more financial support. "I had to think twice before putting my heating on," she says. "It was a horrible, terrible time for the family." Barry, whose husband died two years ago, said she doesn't have much faith in politicians to make the social care system work, but noted the prime minister has experience of the matter as his father has Alzheimer's. "They all make promises but then they never do anything," she said. "I have slightly more confidence in Andy Burnham because he has personal experience of dementia but how is he going to pay for it?" text: Laura Kuenssberg: Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM "You can clap now," a Downing Street official with a clipboard instructed the staff eagerly lining the halls of No 10 in the moments before the new prime minister walked in. The applause duly began before the famous door opened, so the first sight and sound to greet Andy Burnham and his wife were crowds of clapping staff, crammed into the Downing Street hall. They stretched up the long corridor all the way to the door of the Cabinet Room - left ajar for him to walk straight in and get down to work. I've seen plenty of prime ministers come and go from outside No 10. But I'd never been allowed inside at that moment before , able to hover outside the Cabinet Room and grab a quick word with the country's new leader at such an intense, symbolic time. I have rarely seen a politician look as thoroughly delighted as Burnham, pride bursting out of his buttoned-up suit - that's right, the T-shirt and bomber jacket didn't make it to No 10 - or a leader who has wanted to stop and shake as many hands. Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview What kind of prime minister will Andy Burnham be? In his first major broadcast interview since taking office, Laura Kuenssberg asks about his plans - and the challenges ahead. No 10 staff are already wondering if they'll ever be able to stick to a regular prime minister's schedule, normally designed with military precision. If Andy Burnham was able to take the time to stop and speak to everyone in the country, I suspect he probably would. It's a sign of his different style that our team was given permission to be behind the scenes at three key moments in the 59th prime minister's first week in charge - when he became Labour leader, when he walked into No 10, and on day one at his new Manchester outpost, No 10 North. Most important by far was our half-hour interview in that shiny new office, after weeks during which Burnham was chased by accusations he'd avoided tough questions. But the extra glimpses we were given, alongside Burnham's own voracious appetite for social media, display a prime minister that's not just at ease in front of the cameras, but a leader who wants to bring you along for the ride. They included revealing moments that are normally hidden - his first steps into the Cabinet Room to appoint his team, rating pub snacks with his Chancellor, John Healey, in an Instagram post , external , and sharing pictures with us of the family dog, Axel, whom he describes as having "angry little man energy". "Comms" - how politicians communicate and explain themselves and talk to the public - is not the be-all and end-all. Burnham's exploits online have already brought mockery and launched a thousand memes. But if a leader can't get your attention to make their arguments - as Keir Starmer found so challenging - ultimately, they are not going to get very far at all. And the biggest difference of the Labour reboot so far is how the government looks and sounds. They've put an obvious priority on punter-friendly announcements such as cutting VAT from energy bills and tax breaks for pubs - although it is important to note the details on how to pay for all of that are not yet clear. For Burnham though, telling his story is the easy part. Joking about the unique stink that accompanies Scampi Fries, or showing me his gold disc on loan from The Smiths' guitarist Johnny Marr, won't help him deal with US President Donald Trump, find money for defence, or create a new service to care for the elderly and vulnerable in England. Nor will it be any use as he grapples with the country's huge debts, changing demographics or public concerns about immigration. Andy Burnham's dog, Axel Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall. Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times. But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils. Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan". When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024 . But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really? And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt. What about welfare? Remember Sir Keir ditched most significant reforms in the face of resistance on the back benches. While seeking not to "blame" anyone receiving benefits, Burnham said the country had to "get serious" about getting the welfare bill down, and suggested he might make it harder for some people to claim, by imposing extra conditions. He didn't want to give much away about where he was going to find extra billions for defence, or pay for public services. He repeated that he'd stick to the promises on income tax, VAT and National Insurance made in 2024. But the prime minister clearly pointed to a possible shake-up of the council tax system, where those with the most expensive properties might have to pay considerably more. Changes like that to council tax, or to welfare, would be huge political moves that would put him on a collision course with some of his party, and some political opponents too. Then, when it comes to matters of war and peace, which for Burnham are genuinely new, it felt we could see him thinking in real time how to answer the question, perhaps trying to balance giving a flavour of who he is, without creating a political accident. Does he trust Trump? Twice he wouldn't say. "It's a changing world," his second answer. This video can not be played Watch: 'You have to defend your own national interest before anything else' Would he take a call from Russian President, Vladimir Putin? A pause, then: "I'd have to know the circumstances". As mayor, Burnham evidently spent years thinking hard about how to use power, and how he wants to shift the balance in the UK away from Westminster. The impact of that stance could be profound, way beyond some admirably shiny No 10 signs emblazoned all over one floor of a government building in Manchester. Mayors are expected to get power to spend nationally collected income tax, and crucially to spend billions without strings. Burnham spent time too as mayor absorbing people's experiences, their hardships and frustrations. "My strength always is in remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change because I am prime minister," Burnham told me. Although don't be in any doubt, he also spent time thinking and planning about how to make a return to the political heart of this country, the Westminster he believes is so flawed. Andy Burnham with members of his team at the new No 10 North But when it comes to the gravest matters that prime ministers have to deal with - security, power around the world, or the country's long-term economic stability, we're perhaps yet to see if Burnham's ambition for No 10 is accompanied by truly new big ideas that match the scale of his rhetoric. There are worries on the right of the Labour Party that Burnham has not absorbed the reality of the country's economic position - years of stuttering growth, and sky-high levels of debt that leave the UK incredibly vulnerable to the financial markets' judgements, whether he likes it or not. And concerns on the left, that he's tickled their bellies with promises of "authentic Labour", flirting with the ideas of increasing state control of vital industries, but which might not come through. And like most incoming prime ministers, he has precious little experience of handling international events. The moments in our interview where he was least sure-footed were answering questions about how he'd manage relationships with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. Burnham says he is prepared to call out Trump 'if right for Britain' Andy Burnham rules out early election in exclusive BBC interview NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC One minister said he'd "vibe left, but govern from the centre". Perhaps, as he's tried to give firms and families a "breathing space" when it comes to the cost of living, he'll ask for "breathing space" from the public before his complete programme becomes clear. Burnham has long been unusual as a politician - a leader who has managed to be popular in a time when politicians often disappoint and are sometimes despised. He knows he's walking into a job that's been marked by failure for a decade. As he told me, "the onus is on me not to be another one who just doesn't change things". He's part of a political generation he proclaims to be "just not good enough". Remember, his own career has had plenty of failure too. It took Burnham three goes to become the leader of his party. As he arrived, straightening his tie, to be confirmed in the top job in central London 10 days ago, I asked him why he'd taken so long. He laughed and told me, "I like to make an entrance". Andy Burnham has now truly arrived. But he knows all too well, there won't be applause everywhere he goes. text: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to? Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time. He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares. BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about Â£1.5bn. Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line. Cost: Â£340m over five years, funded In his speech outside Downing Street , external on Monday, Burnham said his "first instruction" would be "to end rough sleeping in our country". The most recent official data , external suggests that there were around 4,800 people sleeping rough on a single night in England in 2025, up from 1,800 in 2010. The government announced that Burnham's "instruction" would be delivered by Â£340m of spending, which it said would support at least 3,000 people over a five year period. It said this money would come from existing "uncommitted" budgets in the housing department. This means that the funding has been made available by the Treasury to the department but had not yet been assigned to a specific project. Cost: Â£850m, unfunded On Tuesday morning the Treasury announced that it would cut , external VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, knocking an estimated Â£45 from the typical household's annual bill from the autumn. It said this would cost Â£850m in 2026-27 - to be funded by scrapping the previous government's digital ID scheme, which had been estimated to cost Â£1.8bn over the next three years. However, the Office for Budget Responsibility, the official spending watchdog, made clear in the last budget that the digital ID scheme was itself "unfunded" , external at that stage. That implies that while scrapping the digital ID scheme will reduce a spending pressure on the government it will not, in itself, pay for the VAT cut. That tax cut will have to be funded in the next budget, either by tax rises or specific spending cuts elsewhere. Five headaches Andy Burnham will have to deal with as PM Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high Can Andy Burnham solve the housing crisis? Cost: Â£500m, funded On Wednesday, the government announced it would reduce the cap on bus fares , external in England from Â£3 to Â£2 from 1 January 2027, though this does not include London. It estimated this cap would cost the Department for Transport more than Â£500m. It said most of this would be found by replacing grants for international climate projects with loans. This would save the government money because the loans would be expected to be paid back in full, plus interest, freeing up funds to pay for the bus cap policy. But there are still uncertainties with this approach, said Max Warner from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. "It's not clear how much we would expect to be paid back nor what the interest rates will be," he said. Cost: Â£100m, funded On Thursday the government announced it would cut business rates for pubs , external , clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from April 2027, saving a typical pub Â£1,100. It estimated that this tax cut would cost the Treasury around Â£100m a year. The government claimed it would be "fully funded" but did not provide details, beyond stating that part of the cost would be met by "reviewing reliefs for businesses that do not make a positive contribution to local communities, such as vape shops". It did not state what other kinds of businesses would fall into this category. The Starmer government had already announced a business rates support package , external for pubs in England in January, with a 15% cut applying in the current financial year of 2026-27 and a real-terms freeze in their rates for the subsequent two years. At that time officials estimated that package would cost Â£80m in its first year, and the cost in the subsequent two years would be calculated in due course by the Office for Budget Responsibility. The latest business support for pubs from the Burnham government will come on top of that earlier support - so the Treasury will have to provide an official costing for the overall package announced since January in the Autumn budget. Cost: Downing Street says no additional cost to taxpayers, funded Burnham ended his first week as PM by working out of the new No 10 North , external , based at Heron House in Manchester's city centre, which he claimed will be the "situation room for making Britain better". He's expected to work from there each week, with other ministers including Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster Louise Haigh, who is overseeing the department as part of her role, also working there on a regular basis. Up to 300 civil servants are expected to join the operation by the end of the next year, but Downing Streets insists it will cost taxpayers no extra money. "The running of No 10 North will be covered by existing Cabinet Office budgets. There is no additional cost to taxpayers", Burnham's spokesman told reporters earlier this week. These pledges add up to about Â£1.5bn. That might sound like a lot, but they are small commitments relative to overall government spending, which is projected to be around Â£1.4 trillion (Â£1,400bn) this year - making it about 0.1% of total public spending. The bigger question is whether Burnham is likely to follow through with some of the more expensive policies he's previously signalled, including reforming social care or expanding council house building. Burnham earlier this week indicated he could raise the income tax personal allowance , which the Institute for Fiscal Studies has estimated could end up costing Â£8.5-9bn but the idea of this happening imminently was downplayed within days. Chancellor John Healey is likely to want to take defence spending from 2.7% to 3% of GDP by 2030, given he resigned as Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the Treasury's failure to commit the money to do that. But that would cost an additional Â£9bn a year in today's money. Burnham has also promised the "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period". While the details are unclear, estimates from the Centre for Cities think tanks , external suggest that to match the English council house building rates of the 1950s to the 1970s would require another Â£13bn a year in public subsidy. Policies on this scale, which could run into several billions, would likely need to be set out in future budgets and spending reviews, alongside detailed plans about how they would be paid for. However, Burnham has said he will stick to the government's existing fiscal rules - not borrowing for day-to-day spending and having debt fall as a share of the economy by the end of the Parliament. That means any major new spending commitments would likely require difficult choices: such as raising taxes or cutting spending elsewhere. What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?
title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?

text: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies. From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on. Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies. Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour. These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts. In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons. The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before. What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK. While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles. The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky. At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%). It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived. The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors. The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not. This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains. US hits dozens of countries with new wave of tariffs What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? There should be scope for a better deal for the UK, but it raises an interesting question about whether the government will pursue an EU-style ban. This is widely seen as a backdoor way to target China, in particular for conditions in its Xinjiang province. Last October , external the government said it "remained firmly opposed to the use of state-imposed forced labour", but that it was "considering how best to reflect this position," citing "operational and legal complexities". Since then, the UK has welcomed imports of Chinese cars, and is exploring a services trade deal with the country. The relationship with China has been a balancing act for the government. This is also one of the global stories of the tariff wars. As the US repeatedly changes its rationale for tariffs, the rest of the world is focused on trading with each other. For example, Canada increased its trade with the rest of the world by more than it lost from the US. China's total dollar trade with the US is flat in the first half of this year versus last year. Across the world it is up 21%, including 14% with the EU, 11% with the UK, and 24% with Africa. There could be pressure now to legislate for a formal ban on forced labour products. Successive governments have opted for a lighter voluntary due diligence regime. Will the US force a change in the UK and elsewhere, and what might it offer in return? Or the UK may opt to keep its precarious geopolitical position by sticking to its existing deals in medicines, metals and cars.
title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating

text: Andy Burnham's plan to collaborate with social media creators Young Labour supporters whose TikToks took them to Downing Street Andy Burnham is a past master at using social media to create a political brand - and it seems he has no plans to let up now that he is prime minister. One Downing Street source told the BBC they planned to take a "more social first" and "authentic to Andy" approach, with "less high production, polished" content than might have been seen from a prime minister in the past. This means we can expect more clips of Burnham in casual mode, chatting into a handheld phone or answering questions on policy in an apparently spontaneous fashion on X, Instagram or TikTok. There will also be a focus on collaborations with social media creators. In an earlier age, political leaders liked to court TV stars and other celebrities to help get their message out. Now the Holy Grail is online influencers, who are seen as more authentic, and trusted, by hard-to-reach voters who don't watch much TV or read newspapers. Sir Keir Starmer's government had already begun experimenting with giving access to influencers, with ministers appearing on some of the more popular channels. Downing Street also held receptions for influencers and during Tim Allan's tenure as director of communications content creators were invited to Downing Street press conferences. Some critics saw this is a way of avoiding serious scrutiny of polices in favour of softball questions from non-specialists. But Burnham's advisers see collaborations with influencers as a way of getting the government's message to audiences it might not normally reach. A Downing Street source said "the vast majority" of the public will not see or interact with content that is coming from government or the prime minister's social media channels. Andy Burnham appeared on influencer Max Klymenko's 'career ladder' on his first day as PM In the hours before and after becoming prime minister, Burnham co-authored two posts on TikTok and Instagram, including a running video with Sir Mo Farah. Young TikTokers were also invited to Downing Street to thank them for their work on his Makerfield by-election campaign. One of the social channels Sir Keir Starmer appeared on was run by Ukrainian online personality Max Klymenko, who won TikTok Creator of the year for his viral "The Career Ladder" series, where he quizzes people about their job history. Klymenko was first approached by Burnham's team around two months ago to collaborate on content. His team filmed the video quizzing the former Greater Manchester mayor on his first job, before he entered politics, a week ago, then planned to post it on his first day as prime minister to capitalise on the buzz. The creator's core audience are aged 18 to 24, according to his team, while the majority of people who watch his content are aged between 25 and 30. A member of his team pointed out this is far younger than the audience for a traditional TV interview, while his cumulative subscriber and follower count across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook is more than 16.3 million accounts. While there is some paid-for content on his pages, Klymenko said no payment or contract was exchanged with Burnham's team and they did not request changes to the content before it was posted. Meanwhile, Sir Mo Farah's uploads, running while discussing sport, education and mental health with Burnham, went to his three million followers across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, a far bigger reach than the prime minister's personal channels. Andy Burnham Went Online, and Got Into No 10 Ros Atkins reports on how the new PM uses social media to get his message across. The strategy is the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, who ran Burnham's digital communications during the by-election, and who the BBC can confirm has been kept on for a new role in Burnham's administration. She began her career in social media aged 17 by starting a "Milifandom" campaign on social media for Ed Miliband over a decade ago. In more recent years, she has worked in digital communications for the Labour Party, and for Keir Starmer in Number10 before quitting last year. Tomlinson has been credited with how Burnham connected with voters across platforms in recent months. The new PM has rationed interviews with traditional media since returning to Parliament, in favour of vlogs, a question and answer session on Reddit and X posts clapping back at political opponents. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch took to Reddit to urge him to "come out from hiding, face a proper press conference and submit yourself to scrutiny and some tough questions". Burnham responded to it by saying it had only been two weeks since he faced questions from "74,000 members of the public of Makerfield". Sir Mo Farah put Andy Burnham through his paces on his social media channels Another key strand of Burnham's campaigning strategy has been connecting with and organising grassroots social media activists. Among the politicians and staffers invited to stand outside Number 10 to watch Burnham become prime minister on Monday were teenage TikTokers whose video edits have brought him to a new social media audience. Between them, Will, Lottie, Megan, Ellen and Poppy, all aged between 17 and 19  have racked up millions of likes on TikTok, and across platforms share memes, trends and nostalgic edits of New Labour footage, including of Burnham's time in office. The Labour activists were invited to canvass with him and make edits of his time on the Makerfield by-election campaign trail in a language and style that resonates with people online. One way they got thousands of likes was by getting him to sign and pose with red pre-made cocktails popular with Gen Z. Megan Cassidy, 19, from Havering, started making Labour content a year ago and said it was "surreal" to have found herself at Downing Street: "I really felt like I was witnessing history around me". The young Labour activists said they were given access to Burnham and footage of him by his team, but are not paid and can choose to edit the material how they like. They saw it as an opportunity to gain ground from social media savvy parties like Reform, whose leader Nigel Farage has an exponentially bigger following on social media, and the Greens who have experienced large growth in recent months. It helped that Burnham was "natural" and happy to spontaneously appear in content, they told the BBC. "I do think he gets it, absolutely compared to other politicians, compared to Starmer for example, I think he's a lot more charismatic," said Megan. text: Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM Shortly after Andy Burnham telephoned a number of Keir Starmer's allies to sack them from the cabinet on Monday afternoon, John Healey received the signal to head to Number 10. Wearing a suit and one of his many red ties, the former defence secretary left parliament alone via a back entrance next to a pub. "I'm on my way to a meeting," he said with a slight smile as he marched down Whitehall. Healey's imminent appointment as chancellor was a surprise - to him, to his Labour colleagues, and to the British public. It was a consequential moment among a flurry of announcements from the new prime minister, including today's cut in VAT on energy bills , that demonstrate the new government's intention to move at breakneck speed - at least for now. The Conservatives support that tax cut but have questioned its funding. Five weeks earlier Healey had weakened Keir Starmer's grip on Downing Street by quitting as defence secretary in a row over military spending. Soon he would be back around the cabinet table alongside two others whose recent resignations had also damaged Starmer - new defence secretary Wes Streeting and new energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh. Were they rewarded for rebelling and hastening Burnham's path to office? Possibly. But all three are also widely seen as skilled operators taking on complex roles. This video can not be played Watch: John Healey questioned moments before being made chancellor John Healey's elevation to the second most important job in government has delighted senior figures in the Ministry of Defence, who are relieved to have someone in the Treasury who is committed to increasing military spending. "It's brilliant for us," said an insider. Yet the same MOD source is also relieved Healey is not returning. "We were dreading him coming back", they said. "He's a difficult person". Even some senior Conservatives think Healey's appointment as chancellor was clever. "For a number of reasons", explains one former Tory cabinet minister. "He's not Ed Miliband, he's hard to attack, and he's Treasury-literate." Healey served as a minister in the department for five years during Tony Blair's premiership. Burnham ally Anneliese Midgeley has the difficult task of trying to keep Labour MPs - including those sacked as ministers - loyal to the government. Former chief secretary to the prime minister Darren Jones's public swipe at Burnham's energy bills policy is a sign not all will play nice. One Labour MP claims that those sacked by Burnham can be divided into three groups. "Some went because of their politics, others just weren't good, and then there are those disliked in the parliamentary Labour party," said the MP. Behind the scenes, many in Westminster are talking about the possibility of Burnham taking advantage of a possible bounce in the opinion polls and calling a snap general election. Nigel Farage wants one and argues it is necessary since Burnham has no mandate. But with the Reform leader facing both a by-election and questions over his finances, some in his party worry that if Burnham moves too fast, Farage could miss his one great chance to become PM. "We are really worried about a snap election," said the Reform source, grinning. "Which is why we're calling for a snap election." Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey were among the winners in Burnham's reshuffle Across all the parties at Westminster, plans are being put in place in case a snap contest is called. "We've started preparing," said a senior Liberal Democrat aide. Burnham has appeared to rule out heading to the polls. It would certainly anger some Labour MPs who could lose their seats. Yet it would also offer the new PM an opportunity to get a fresh mandate for more radical policies, as well as secure his position for a full five year term. "There is economic pain coming down the horizon", says the former Conservative cabinet minister. "And it's about how far he [Burnham] gets ahead of it. He faces a choice between going for an election, and a slow decline as we saw with Gordon Brown." That former PM was dubbed "bottler Brown" in 2007 after considering going to the polls before deciding against it. Yet Brown got to Number 10 with a mixture of patience, caution, guile and ruthlessness, whereas Burnham's speedy rise was largely due to one major electoral gamble. After his success in Makerfield and then the Labour leadership contest, will Burnham fancy another throw of the dice? Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet? text: Prisoner release row proving to be Burnham's first big test as PM Three weeks into his premiership, Andy Burnham has "hit bumps in the road" in the estimation of one long-serving Labour MP with the row over the early release of some prisoners from jail. His political opponents are already sharpening their attacks, believing they have found an issue with which to discomfit a new prime minister early in his time in office who had, until now, displayed a pretty deft political touch. Conservative Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "This the most important decision Andy Burnham has made since he became prime minister and he's got it wrong." For Labour MPs, however, this week has shown Burnham is prepared to confront difficult choices and take decisions which, as he said in his first speech in Downing Street, are "more about problem solving than point scoring". Burnham's first two weeks in the job were pretty problem free, with a succession of announcements, from a cap on bus fares to a determination to overhaul of social care, along with a blitz of social media videos, all designed to portray a more relaxed PM with a focus on everyday issues. The overcrowding crisis in our prisons has presented him with a dilemma for which there are only unpalatable choices. Crucially too, they are some of the first difficult choices Burnham has had to make in office. The issue long predates his arrival in Downing Street. In 2023, with space in jails on the verge of running out, the last Conservative government started releasing prisoners 18 days early. That was only a temporary fix. Just days after becoming prime minister in July 2024, Sir Keir Starmer had to contemplate a more far-reaching prisoner release scheme, saying "it is shocking for our country to have got into a state where we have too many prisoners and not enough prison places". In January this year, Sir Keir's government passed the Sentencing Act under which several thousand prisoners will be released early starting this autumn, including some convicted of very serious crimes. HMP Wandsworth, in London, is Britain's most overcrowded prison Andy Burnham, aware of how sensitive this would be, immediately ordered a review. His frustration was evident when he announced he was removing some categories of prisoner from early release, rapists and child sex offenders among them, but not others. "The truth is I wanted to go even further," he said, "I have pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do". The Conservatives seized on the fact that his decisions mean that among those still being let out early will be some who committed grooming-related crimes as well as some killers, including those of PC Andrew Harper. "The Labour government has made mistake after mistake on this early release scheme," said Chris Philp. "Despite our warnings in Parliament, they initially planned to release rapists and dangerous criminals. "But, even after Andy Burnham's review, it turns out they still plan to release cop-killers and men involved in the grooming gang scandal early. It's an insult to PC Harper's family and many other victims." Up against Sir Keir, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch managed to find issues she could use to force him on to the back foot and into what turned out to be a damaging series of policy shifts. She has seized on the early releases to do try to do the same with his successor. A first sign of that came when Burnham had to "personally intervene" this week, his spokesperson said, to order officials to find out how many people convicted of grooming-related offences might still be getting early release. That came after Badenoch highlighted the issue in an open letter to him. The Conservatives are now considering how they can keep the pressure up when parliament returns in September. They will aim to place Labour MPs in an uncomfortable position if the issue can be debated in the Commons. What's behind having to release some prisoners early? Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early Burnham orders review of grooming gang early releases Justice secretary apologises to families affected by early release scheme Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy has called on the government to introduce "emergency primary legislation as soon as Parliament returns in September," as he says that is the only way to permanently exclude "killers - like the killers of PC Harper - child abusers and grooming gang members from early release". For now, Labour MPs are off on their summer breaks. "There is no point in bemoaning what is going on" one says phlegmatically, "Andy Burnham's inherited this vexed issue that our jails are full, it's in the nature of being PM.". "I have every confidence in him. Over all the years Andy Burnham has never been fearful of speaking to victims directly," adds the MP who has served on the justice select committee. But they added: "We need to have an honest conversation about who we are sending to jail as we don't have the spaces to accommodate everyone we are sending." Another MP, from the left of the party, said Labour members still felt overwhelmingly positive about their new leader despite the row over prisoner releases. "They don't believe he has a magic wand. I don't blame him for the overcrowding crisis and I don't think voters do". And the MP added "at least we have a recognisably Labour government. It feels like we are in play again, with a second chance to make a difference, maybe even to win a second term". text: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election. Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down. But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence. The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented. All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 â which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II â failed to give her party a boost. It is not unusual for a new prime minister to enjoy a poll bounce We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term â even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office. Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election. That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election â and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling. But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity. Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August. This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign. In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process. But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls. The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens â much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters â the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving. When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%. Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street. Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring. Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. But despite having overtaken Reform in the polls, the new Labour leader still has to prove he can win back the working class pro-Brexit voters that Labour once regarded as its core vote but who now form the heart of support for Reform. To do this â and put Labour on course for victory in 2029 - Burnham needs to deliver on the policy challenges facing his government, which remain as formidable as those that beset Sir Keir. Labour's prospects at the next election will ultimately depend on whether voters have come to believe that what he has said he will do is actually happening. text: Key takeaways as Andy Burnham becomes PM Andy Burnham has replaced Sir Keir Starmer as UK prime minister, after becoming Labour leader last week. The former mayor of Greater Manchester becomes the country's fourth prime minister in five years and the seventh since 2016. Live: Andy Burnham sets out his priorities as prime minister In his first speech in Downing Street, Burnham announced he would "end rough sleeping in our country". This was swiftly followed by a No 10 press release promising an extra Â£340m for the task over the next five years from within the housing department budget. He also promised a new 10-year plan for Britain - to be unveiled later this year - and to build a new economy, putting "life's essentials back under public control". But arguing that people also needed "breathing space now", he said announcements on tackling the cost of living would start on Tuesday. Other changes he promised included changing the education system to help young people into work, building more council homes, and honouring commitments to fund defence while sticking to the UK's spending and debt rules. Burnham pledges to end rough sleeping in first speech as prime minister Burnham promises help with your money. How could it affect you? Burnham made top appointments to his cabinet, making John Healey his chancellor in an move that took Westminster by surprise. Rachel Reeves had already confirmed she would be leaving the role and would not be serving in Burnham's cabinet, turning down the offer of another job. In other top moves, former energy secretary Ed Miliband has been promoted to foreign secretary, with Shabana Mahmood reappointed home secretary. Louise Haigh, a key ally who oversaw his preparations for No 10, has been given the job of running the Cabinet Office and appointed first secretary of state. Appointments, including to roles below the cabinet rank, are expected to continue on Tuesday. Watch: Starmer resigns, Burnham becomes PM... the day so far 'A circuit-breaker moment' - Watch Andy Burnham's first speech as PM in full There was much that was familiar about Burnham's speech in front of the famous black No 10 door, which was thronged with staffers and supporters. But perhaps conscious that "lectern moments" have become a symbol of the UK's political instability in recent years, Burnham broke with recent tradition and made the address without notes or a podium. He said that he was "acutely conscious" of the churn in the office behind him, stressing that the UK badly needed to regain stability. This would require politicians to "make politics work better" and "raise our game and rise to the new challenge", he added. Andy Burnham: Who is the new PM? From Manchester mayor to prime minister; what is his record and what does he stand for? Who is Andy Burnham's wife, Marie-France van Heel? King Charles III said his farewells to Sir Keir in a final private audience at Buckingham Palace, before greeting Burnham. His role was central to the day because prime ministers are formally appointed by the sitting monarch, who is head of state. The short audience is known as "kissing hands" - although in practice, these days male premiers simply bow and shake hands with the monarch after accepting their offer to form a government. Earlier, Sir Keir gave a short departure speech in Downing Street. With his supporters lining the street, he repeated key themes from the speech announcing his resignation in June, such as turning around the fortunes of the Labour Party and lowering child poverty. Despite leaving just two years after his landslide victory at the 2024 election, he insisted that he was proud of his record in office, saying Britain was "now stronger and fairer". "I go with good grace, I go with a smile," he said. He had time for a hug afterwards with Rachel Reeves, his chancellor and Downing Street neighbour during his time in office. What questions do you have about the new PM and his policies?
title: Key takeaways as Andy Burnham becomes PM

text: Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? Up until this point, the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described his policy changes with a broad brush. From today, he faces the constraints, trade offs, and realities of high national office. For example, Burnham has said Tuesday's announcements on cost of living support would be paid for. In other words, it would mean a tax rise or spending cut, so we will see rather quickly what the new PM prioritises when push comes to shove. Meanwhile, the markets seem to have already reacted to the suggestion he would be using some "flexibility" in his borrowing rules to help with new announcements. The UK government's 10-year borrowing rose above 5% on Monday after falling in recent days. It has not gone up in this way in other European economies. The move was not huge, but it shows the sensitivities at a moment when Burnham is overhauling his cabinet - including replacing Rachel Reeves as chancellor with former defence secretary John Healey. The "flexibility" Burnham was talking about is, I understand, about the treatment of financial institutions. This has occurred in some green energy policies and essentially helps exempt certain types of borrowing from the measures of debt. There is scope for this model to extend to housing and other infrastructure. It was not a general suggestion of, for example, using up the increased headroom against the government's borrowing rules. All this shows how every tricky decision and trade off is being watched by the country and the markets at the same time. Healey is a surprise choice as chancellor but perhaps should not have been. He spent half a decade in Gordon Brown's treasury with specific knowledge of that era's attempt to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government. No 10 is stressing that Burnham and Healey "have the same outlook" on the need to maintain economic stability and the current fiscal rules, reindustrialisation, devolution, helping people with the cost-of-living crisis and backing British jobs and British industry to drive growth across the country. But immediately there is a trade-off here. Healey resigned as defence secretary last month over funding the defence settlement. He was literally calling for more defence spending, and some of the previous increases in defence funding came from cutting back home infrastructure spending on transport and on energy investment. How will he square those things as chancellor? In his first comments as chancellor, Healey has told broadcasters that he will work "in lockstep" with the new PM "to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty", and making life more affordable. He had revealed he had just spoken to Andrew Bailey the Bank of England governor. Overall, Healey will probably calm any market jitters after Monday's uptick in government borrowing rates. He quickly has to deliver a funded cost of living policy. On policy, Burnham's camp has floated the idea of unfreezing the income tax threshold â and I'm taking it pretty seriously that this may happen. Some big unions have swung behind the idea, which would cost at least Â£4bn depending on the rate of inflation. And others have floated the idea of not just unfreezing the thresholds in 2027 â lifting it from the current Â£12,570 basic rate to Â£13,000 and at the upper end from Â£50,271 to Â£52,000 â but rolling it back to what it would have been if the freeze hadn't been implemented in 2022. This would be much more expensive to do. The UK is in the middle of a nine-year threshold freeze announced by then-chancellor Rishi Sunak to repay the billions borrowed to fund the Covid lockdown. The freeze was extended at the last Budget by Rachel Reeves until 2030-31, pushing one in six workers into the 40p bracket. It is intriguing that Burnham says this came up on Makerfield doorstep, as is the fact that significant unions now prioritise a policy that affects their members on or around Â£50,000 a year. We're talking the likes of nurses, midwives, paramedics, teachers, and engineers. However, as some current Number 10 insiders have pointed to, it adds to a list of net spending policies and raises questions about the extent of tax rises or extra borrowing required to make Budget sums add up. Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK? More widely, Burnham has also said he would publish a 10-year plan for the country and the economy later this year, likely to detail his wider plans on decentralisation, devolution, and rebuilding Britain. Ordinarily, you might expect a significant infrastructure programme with such plans, but Burnham also wants to fund the Defence Investment Plan, a multi-billion, multi-year spending commitment for the UK military. How will he square this? In addition, his first priority going through the doors, he said, would be a national plan to end rough sleeping. He made a similar pledge in Greater Manchester, but some early progress went in reverse in recent years. When I questioned him about this in February, he said more funding and powers from central government were needed to deal with the recent rise. As his first act as PM, he has now released funds to address it from within the housing budget. Long term, he said the answer is mass council house building. This will take years to feed through. Welfare is another critical test. Here, I'm told, Burnham expects to show he can make progress on what he called "sustainable reform". This will lean heavily on Alan Milburn's review, which is likely to recommend significant job support funds and mental health assistance for young workers in order to reduce welfare bills. This is likely to be delivered by local mayors who know what works in their regions. Burnham hopes to show the markets he can deliver the welfare reform that eluded former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. This is the new PM's conundrum. He faces the same manifesto and borrowing rule constraints as his predecessor, yet he clearly wants to do more. He says his rewiring of Britain will help the economy grow, but many of these solutions could take years. And the recent rapid turnover of prime ministers and chancellors shows, even thinking a few years ahead might feel like a luxury. Andy Burnham: Who is the new PM? text: Can Burnham's casual style survive contact with No 10? Andy Burnham has lots to think about as his arrival in Downing Street draws closer - the cost of living, the ongoing war in Ukraine, how to fund defence to name just three. At some point though, he'll have to find time to decide what to wear. The MP for Makerfield has sometimes been accused of changing his political clothes, and on his journey from Manchester to London, he changed his actual clothes. He boarded the train at Manchester Piccadilly in his trademark dark T-shirt, trousers and Adidas trainers only to emerge, more than two hours later, at London Euston in a suit. Twenty minutes later, he turned up in Parliament, having added a tie to his ensemble. Was this wardrobe change a symbolic gesture - Burnham signalling that with his move from Greater Manchester mayor to prime minister he would be adopting a more formal style in the job? Or was it a one-off, with Burnham planning to maintain his "Manchester clothes" - which have been variously described as "normcore," "centrist dad" and "The Smiths meets Britpop" - once he gets the keys to No 10. Emma Finamore, features editor at Drapers Magazine has dubbed Burnham , external "the king of the casuals". His look is considered "smart" but "less formal than other politicians", she says. "It's aspirational but attainable. A lot of the stuff he wears isn't outside the realm of possibility." Harrington jackets, high-street staples such as polo shirts from Uniqlo and  Wallabees from Clarks, are often part of the "smart-Manc" costume, characterised by a deliberate departure from the traditional suit-and-tie uniform of the SW1 postcode. But if he does return to ties and suits as prime minister, it will only be a regression to his previous Westminster look. Pre-2020, Burnham was more often seen in a suit than without one. In photos from his second Labour leadership campaign in 2015, he is suited and booted sitting next to one of his rival candidates, the far more casual Jeremy Corbyn. The tie-less, suit-less Corbyn romped to victory in that contest, beating Burnham into second place. After leaving Westminster, Burnham similarly began to dispense with ties and jackets. Speaking to the Guardian in 2022, he said: "I remember, when I left, slowly realising: 'I don't have to do this any more.' "What I would have worn to the match at weekends, I just started wearing. It was an evolution and I'm not going back." His Howick jacket - the one he wore when making his angry intervention in the Covid lockdown debates - has become an exhibit in Manchester's People's History Museum. Finamore says Burnham is "a savvy enough politician to know when he can wear some things and when he can't. He will have to abide by dress codes. "I don't think he will go back fully. He has got that confidence. He seems to have found his political identity and also his style as mayor of Greater Manchester." One place he will have to abide by a formal dress code is in the House of Commons. The previous Speaker, John Bercow, relaxed the rules, telling MPs they didn't need to wear a tie, but his successor Sir Lindsay Hoyle is having none of it. Speaking at his summer reception for Westminster journalists, he said: "King of the North or not, unless Andy Burnham swaps his dark T-shirt for a shirt and tie, in my Kingdom, he's not going to get called." Burnham's "Manchester clothes" are also unlikely to wash at the White House. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's decision to eschew suits for military-style clothing is driven by his desire to show solidarity for soldiers fighting the Russians. But it annoyed some Americans and his attire was a factor in the infamous bust-up between Zelensky, Trump and his Vice President JD Vance in the Oval Office. The pussy-bow blouse became a hallmark of Margaret Thatcher's signature style, blending traditionally feminine fashion with a carefully crafted image of authority It may seem trivial, but clothes do matter in politics. As previous British prime ministers, particularly Harold Wilson and Margaret Thatcher, have showed, fashion can be used as a powerful political tool. Renowned for her signature wardrobe of high-shoulder suits, pussy-bow blouses, and her iconic handbag, Thatcher cultivated an image that sought to project a sense of authority and purpose. In contrast, Wilson - often anchored by his ever-present pipe and Gannex coat - was famed for a pragmatic, utilitarian wardrobe that defined the "cloth-cap" socialism of the 1960s and 70s. The dress sense of female politicians, says Rob Ford, professor of political science at the University of Manchester, comes under much more scrutiny than that of their male counterparts. "There's an enormous double standard with this," Ford says. "It's harder for a female politician because you've got to make choices all the time." At least men can always fall back on suits, he says. Image isn't everything though, as Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued last month, when she dismissed Burnham as "a pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt". In a video responding to her dig, Burnham looked down at his T-shirt before saying: "It's not black, it's dark navy." In a speech made after he was confirmed as the new Labour leader this week, Burnham - wearing a suit and tie - could not resist bringing up his clothes again. Labour, he said, had worn "too many Tory clothes" in the past. "Let me tell you - I'm quite happy that Kemi doesn't approve of my wardrobe choices â because I'm not keen on theirs either," Burnham said. "From here, we do it differently." Ironically, Sir Keir Starmer had also embraced the dress-down spirit of his successor, with the outgoing PM sometimes seen in tracksuits, a Stone Island polo shirt, and Adidas trainers. The difference, says Prof Rob Ford, is that Burnham's fashion choices have cut through with the public. "The fact people have noticed he has a distinctive manner of dress is a victory for his branding efforts," Ford says. Like Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, Burnham likes to be photographed swigging pints in pubs. "The aim of his clothes is similar - to say I'm not a professional politician, I'm one of you," Ford says. Retaining that approachable, homespun persona while adhering to the sartorial conventions and expectations of Westminster will be a challenge for Burnham. In an era when politics has never been more visual, he'll need to dress to impress, whatever he decides to wear.
